USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the current negotiation track without new escalations. The Beijing talks just concluded constructively (extended to an unscheduled third day), and Vice Premier Liu He is expected in Washington later this month. The March 2 deadline provides natural leverage — there is no need to add pressure now when time is working in our favor. Maintain the existing tariff posture on $250B of Chinese goods while the purchase-track and structural-reform discussions advance.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of -0.3 (mild opportunity) reflects asymmetric leverage in our favor. China's manufacturing PMI contracted in December (49.4, below 50 for the first time since mid-2016), new export orders shrank for a seventh straight month (46.6), and Q3 2018 GDP hit 6.5% — the slowest since 2009. Their stock market fell ~25% in 2018 and the yuan depreciated ~5% against the dollar (Reuters, Dec 31 2018; World Bank China Economic Update, Dec 2018). China is under more economic pain than the US from this dispute, which gives us negotiating leverage.

However, this is not a -0.8 or -1.0 opportunity because US domestic conditions are deteriorating too. The S&P 500 had its worst December since 1931 (CNN, Dec 18), Richmond Fed manufacturing plunged to -8 in the largest monthly drop in survey history, Dallas Fed business activity fell to -5.1, and consumer confidence posted its sharpest monthly decline in three years (Yahoo Finance, Dec 31). Multiple S&P 500 companies have issued earnings warnings, and analysts project single-digit earnings growth for the next three quarters (CNBC, Jan 9). The partial government shutdown adds further uncertainty.

The action stance of -0.1 (hold/negotiate, very slightly firm) reflects the judgment that the current posture is working: we have tariffs covering ~$250B of Chinese imports, the 90-day clock runs to March 2, and the just-concluded Beijing talks produced constructive signals without requiring new commitments from our side. China has made goodwill gestures (resumed soybean purchases, approved five GMO crop imports, suspended auto tariffs). But the hard issues — forced technology transfer, IP enforcement, industrial subsidies, verification mechanisms — remain unresolved (PBS, Jan 9; Guardian, Jan 9). Pushing for escalation now would risk rattling already-fragile markets and hardening Beijing's nationalist posture, especially given the Huawei/Meng situation which has inflamed Chinese public opinion. Better to let Liu He come to Washington, see what the purchase track yields, and reserve escalation for the structural-reform phase if China proves unwilling to move on those issues.
key_factors: China manufacturing PMI contracted to 49.4 in December 2018 (below 50 for first time since mid-2016)
US stock market worst December since 1931; multiple Fed manufacturing surveys plunged in December
Beijing trade talks extended to 3rd day, described as constructive — progress on purchases, structural issues remain open
March 2 deadline for tariff hike from 10% to 25% on $200B provides natural leverage
Huawei Meng Wanzhou arrest inflamed Chinese nationalism; risk of hardening Beijing stance
China resumed US soybean purchases and approved GMO crop imports as goodwill gestures
US government partial shutdown adding domestic economic uncertainty
72 S&P 500 companies issued Q4 earnings warnings

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended.
Trade talks resume in Beijing (working / mid-level). China discusses increased purchases of US goods; structural issues remain open.
Talks extended for an unscheduled third day, fueling optimism. Trump tweeted: Talks with China are going very well!
China official manufacturing PMI fell to 49.4 in December — first contraction since July 2016. New export orders shrank for seventh straight month at 46.6.
Dow and S&P 500 each down about 7.8% in December — largest drop since 1931. Stocks on track for worst annual loss since 2008.

Richmond Fed manufacturing reading dropped to -8 (largest month-on-month decline in history). Dallas Fed business activity plunged to -5.1. Consumer confidence hit six-month low with largest monthly drop in three years.
Neither side has given any indication its basic position has changed. The U.S. demands strike at the heart of a state-led development model.
